question: What is the main job of haemostasis in the human body?

options.A: To increase blood pressure during shock
options.B: To speed up the flow of red blood cells
options.C: To stop bleeding after a vessel gets injured
options.D: To destroy unwanted bacteria in the blood

explanation: Think of haemostasis as your body's natural emergency repair team! Its main job is to stop bleeding and patch up damaged blood vessels. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h1)

question: What is formed at the very end of the clotting process to firmly seal a damaged blood vessel?
explanation: At the finish line of the clotting cascade, fibrinogen turns into a strong, stable fibrin mesh that holds the blood clot firmly in place like a net. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h1)

question: How do medicines like tranexamic acid help control bleeding?

options.A: By thinning the blood to prevent blockages
options.B: By destroying extra platelets in the spleen
options.C: By stopping blood clots from breaking down too early
options.D: By increasing the heart rate during trauma

explanation: These drugs act like a protective shield for your clots, stopping the body from dissolving them before the wound is fully healed. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h2)

question: What is Vitamin K's main role when it comes to blood clotting?

options.A: It dissolves dangerous blood clots in the veins
options.B: It helps the liver produce important clotting proteins
options.C: It constricts damaged blood vessels instantly
options.D: It stimulates the bone marrow to make platelets

explanation: Vitamin K is like a helper vitamin that your liver needs to build essential clotting factors. Without it, your blood cannot clot properly! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h2)

question: Why is desmopressin often given to patients with mild hemophilia A?

options.A: It dissolves unwanted clots in the brain
options.B: It releases stored Factor VIII into the bloodstream
options.C: It stops the liver from making extra bile
options.D: It lowers high blood pressure during surgery

explanation: Desmopressin gives a helpful nudge to your body to release extra Factor VIII, which boosts your ability to form clots. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h3)

question: A patient taking warfarin has a dangerously high INR and mild bleeding. What will the medical team most likely give?
explanation: Since warfarin blocks Vitamin K, giving extra Vitamin K is the direct antidote to reverse its effects and restore normal clotting. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h3)

question: What is the big advantage of using topical haemostatic agents during surgery?

options.A: They control bleeding right at the specific wound site
options.C: They cure inherited blood disorders permanently
options.D: They thin the blood throughout the entire body

explanation: Topical means 'applied locally'! These agents go straight onto the bleeding surface to stop the flow right where it's happening. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h4)

question: How do fibrin sealants work when you put them on bleeding tissue?

options.A: They numb nerve endings to stop pain
options.B: They permanently dilate local blood vessels
options.C: They lower the local body temperature
options.D: They mimic the final step of the natural clotting process

explanation: Fibrin sealants bring ready-to-use clotting ingredients straight to the wound, acting like a biological glue that creates an instant clot. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h4)

question: Why shouldn't you give anti-bleeding (antihaemorrhagic) drugs to a patient who already has active blood clots?

options.A: It lowers their blood pressure too quickly
options.B: It stops the liver from making albumin
options.C: It prevents the kidneys from filtering urine
options.D: It can cause dangerous new clots in vital organs

explanation: If a patient is already forming unwanted clots, giving drugs that promote clotting is like pouring fuel on a fire—it can cause dangerous blockages! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h5)

question: In which of these situations is it UNSAFE to give standard anti-bleeding drugs?
explanation: A deep vein thrombosis means a clot is already stuck where it shouldn't be. Adding an anti-bleeding drug here puts the patient at high risk. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h5)

question: What is the most serious risk when a patient takes anti-bleeding medications?

options.D: Unwanted blood clots traveling in the vessels

explanation: Because these drugs push the body to clot, overdoing it can cause clots to form and travel where they shouldn't, leading to serious trouble. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h6)

question: A patient receiving an anti-bleeding drug suddenly gets short of breath and has chest pain. What should the nurse suspect?

options.B: A sudden drop in body temperature

explanation: Chest pain and sudden shortness of breath are classic red flags for a pulmonary embolism—a clot that has traveled to the lungs. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h6)

question: Which lab results are most important for a nurse to check before starting a patient on anti-bleeding therapy?

options.A: Clotting profiles like PT, INR, and aPTT

explanation: Always check your patient's clotting baseline! Tests like PT, INR, and aPTT tell you how their blood is currently handling coagulation. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h7)

question: A patient is receiving an anti-bleeding infusion. What is the most critical thing for the nurse to keep watching for?

options.A: Testing urine sugar levels after every meal
options.B: Watching for signs of abnormal blood clots and ongoing bleeding
options.C: Checking their eyesight every two hours
options.D: Checking daily weight changes for fluid retention

explanation: As a nurse, you walk a fine line: you want to make sure the bleeding stops, but you also must watch closely for signs of dangerous new clots forming! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h7)
